1: //! Chunk-instanced vista tree cards.
2: //!
3: //! A dense woodland vista resolves to tens of thousands of whole-tree
4: //! billboards - measured at 29,247 for `dense-woodland`, nearly all of them in
5: //! the 250 m LOD ring. As one entity each they dominated
6: //! `check_visibility_cpu_culling`, which sweeps every renderable entity once
7: //! per frame and runs serially on wasm. Chunked, the same stands cost one
8: //! entity per distinct card variant per wide ground cell.
9: //!
10: //! Every per-card difference fits `ChunkInstance`: position and uniform scale,
11: //! with no rotation at all (the shader yaws each card to the camera). The one
12: //! value that did not fit is the near cutoff, which scales with the card's own
13: //! height; `tactical_vista_tree_instanced.wgsl` evaluates it per instance.
14: 
15: use bevy::{
16:     ecs::system::SystemParam,
17:     prelude::{Asset, Assets, Commands, Handle, Image, Mesh, Name, ResMut, TypePath, Vec4},
18:     render::render_resource::{
19:         AsBindGroup, RenderPipelineDescriptor, SpecializedMeshPipelineError,
20:     },
21:     shader::ShaderRef,
22: };
23: 
24: use crate::presentation::chunk_instancing::{
25:     ChunkInstance, ChunkInstancedMaterial, ChunkSize, FadeBand, InstanceBatch, InstanceReach,
26:     enable_alpha_to_coverage,
27: };
28: 
29: use super::{VistaLod, VistaTerrain};
30: use crate::presentation::obstacles::tree::TacticalTreeImpostorMaterial;
31: 
32: const VISTA_TREE_SHADER: &str = "shaders/tactical_vista_tree_instanced.wgsl";
33: /// Vista rings span kilometres of sparse stands; wide cells keep the entity
34: /// count low enough for serial CPU culling on wasm.
35: const VISTA_CARD_CHUNK_SIZE: ChunkSize = ChunkSize(256.0);
36: 
37: /// Instanced twin of `TacticalTreeImpostorMaterial`, restricted to the
38: /// whole-tree camera-facing representation every vista stand uses.
39: #[derive(Asset, TypePath, AsBindGroup, Debug, Clone)]
40: pub(in crate::presentation) struct TacticalVistaTreeInstancedMaterial {
41:     #[texture(0)]
42:     #[sampler(1)]
43:     pub(in crate::presentation) baked_color: Handle<Image>,
44:     /// Unscaled card height, deterministic seed, wind strength, wind speed.
45:     /// The per-entity material carried the representation level in x; every
46:     /// vista card is level 4, so x now carries the height the near cutoff
47:     /// needs.
48:     #[uniform(2)]
49:     pub(in crate::presentation) parameters: Vec4,
50:     #[uniform(2)]
51:     pub(in crate::presentation) lighting: Vec4,
52:     #[uniform(2)]
53:     pub(in crate::presentation) ambient: Vec4,
54: }
55: 
56: impl ChunkInstancedMaterial for TacticalVistaTreeInstancedMaterial {
57:     fn shader() -> ShaderRef {
58:         VISTA_TREE_SHADER.into()
59:     }
60: 
61:     fn specialize(
62:         descriptor: &mut RenderPipelineDescriptor,
63:         _layout: &bevy::mesh::MeshVertexBufferLayoutRef,
64:         _key: Self::Data,
65:     ) -> Result<(), SpecializedMeshPipelineError> {
66:         // Cards are two-sided and cut out of the atlas through coverage.
67:         descriptor.primitive.cull_mode = None;
68:         enable_alpha_to_coverage(descriptor);
69:         Ok(())
70:     }
71: }
72: 
73: /// The two material stores a vista card batch draws from, as one parameter so
74: /// the caller's signature does not grow with the instanced twin.
75: #[derive(SystemParam)]
76: pub(in crate::presentation) struct VistaTreeMaterials<'w> {
77:     pub(in crate::presentation) impostor: ResMut<'w, Assets<TacticalTreeImpostorMaterial>>,
78:     pub(in crate::presentation) cards: ResMut<'w, Assets<TacticalVistaTreeInstancedMaterial>>,
79: }
80: 
81: /// Collects instances per distinct card variant while the lattice is walked.
82: #[derive(Default)]
83: pub(super) struct VistaCardBatches {
84:     groups: Vec<VistaCardGroup>,
85: }
86: 
87: struct VistaCardGroup {
88:     mesh: Handle<Mesh>,
89:     source: Handle<TacticalTreeImpostorMaterial>,
90:     card_height: f32,
91:     instances: Vec<ChunkInstance>,
92: }
93: 
94: impl VistaCardBatches {
95:     pub(super) fn push(
96:         &mut self,
97:         mesh: &Handle<Mesh>,
98:         source: &Handle<TacticalTreeImpostorMaterial>,
99:         card_height: f32,
100:         instance: ChunkInstance,
101:     ) {
102:         if let Some(group) = self
103:             .groups
104:             .iter_mut()
105:             .find(|group| &group.source == source && &group.mesh == mesh)
106:         {
107:             group.instances.push(instance);
108:             return;
109:         }
110:         self.groups.push(VistaCardGroup {
111:             mesh: mesh.clone(),
112:             source: source.clone(),
113:             card_height,
114:             instances: vec![instance],
115:         });
116:     }
117: 
118:     /// Spawns chunks per variant. `far_band` is the LOD ring's fade-out;
119:     /// the near end stays zero because the shader applies each card's own
120:     /// cutoff, which varies with its instance scale.
121:     pub(super) fn spawn(
122:         self,
123:         commands: &mut Commands<'_, '_>,
124:         lod: &VistaLod,
125:         materials: &mut VistaTreeMaterials<'_>,
126:     ) {
127:         // Cards in a ring share the ring's fade-out; only the near cutoff
128:         // varies per card, and the shader derives that from the instance scale.
129:         let far = super::vista_tree_visibility(lod.spacing_metres, 1.0, 1.0).end_margin;
130:         let level = lod.level;
131:         for group in self.groups {
132:             let Some(source) = materials.impostor.get(&group.source) else {
133:                 continue;
134:             };
135:             let material = materials.cards.add(TacticalVistaTreeInstancedMaterial {
136:                 baked_color: source.baked_color.clone(),
137:                 parameters: Vec4::new(
138:                     group.card_height,
139:                     source.parameters.y,
140:                     source.parameters.z,
141:                     source.parameters.w,
142:                 ),
143:                 lighting: source.lighting,
144:                 ambient: source.ambient,
145:             });
146:             InstanceBatch {
147:                 mesh: group.mesh,
148:                 material,
149:                 instances: group.instances,
150:                 band: FadeBand::until(far.clone()),
151:                 // Cards turn to face the camera, so their width reaches as
152:                 // far as their height in every direction.
153:                 reach: InstanceReach {
154:                     horizontal: group.card_height,
155:                     above: group.card_height,
156:                     below: 0.0,
157:                 },
158:                 chunk_size: VISTA_CARD_CHUNK_SIZE,
159:             }
160:             .spawn(commands, |chunk| {
161:                 (
162:                     Name::new(format!("Instanced vista tree cards ({})", chunk.len())),
163:                     VistaTerrain(level),
164:                     super::VistaTreePresentation,
165:                 )
166:             });
167:         }
168:     }
169: }

1: //! Shared pure vista tuft preparation and renderer installation.
2: use super::*;
3: use crate::presentation::ground_scatter::{
4:     GrassWorld, MINIMUM_GRASS_SLOPE_NORMAL_Y, TierSpeciesBatches, TuftPigment, TuftPlacement,
5:     grass_scatter_density, scatter_cell_tufts, spawn_tuft_batches,
6: };
7: use adventuresim_building_generator::spatial_geometry::PositiveLength;
8: use adventuresim_tactical_core::{
9:     city_layout::grounding::{SupportElevation, SupportQuery},
10:     scene_coordinates::ScenePlanPoint,
11: };
12: use fabelgeist_determinism::Seed;
13: 
14: /// Instance placement for the vista rings: the same tuft lattice as the
15: /// playable sward. Owned scenes sample height from accepted physical support;
16: /// sampled scenes use the presented vista heightfield. Coverage comes from the
17: /// boundary-stitched ground cover. Sites inside the playable rectangle report
18: /// bare so the two swards tile without overlapping.
19: struct VistaTuftPlacement<'a> {
20:     lod: &'a VistaLod,
21:     coarser_lod: Option<&'a VistaLod>,
22:     playable_half_extent: Vec2,
23:     playable_terrain: &'a SceneTerrain,
24:     playable_ground: &'a SceneGround,
25:     urban_ground: &'a UrbanGround,
26:     profile: GrassCommunityProfile,
27:     communities: GrassCommunityField,
28:     /// How far past the playable rectangle this sward reaches, in metres.
29:     outer_collar: f32,
30: }
31: 
32: impl TuftPlacement for VistaTuftPlacement<'_> {
33:     fn lattice_bounds(&self, cell_spacing: f32) -> (IVec2, IVec2) {
34:         let outer = self.playable_half_extent + Vec2::splat(self.outer_collar);
35:         (
36:             (-outer / cell_spacing).floor().as_ivec2(),
37:             (outer / cell_spacing).ceil().as_ivec2(),
38:         )
39:     }
40: 
41:     /// `coverage` clears the playable interior per tuft, which is what keeps
42:     /// the boundary exact. Rejecting cells that sit wholly inside it as well is
43:     /// pure speed: those cells would query support height once per tuft only
44:     /// to discard every one.
45:     fn cell_allows(&self, _cell_hash: Seed, cell: IVec2, cell_spacing: f32, _jitter: f32) -> bool {
46:         let centre = cell.as_vec2() * cell_spacing;
47:         let interior = self.playable_half_extent - Vec2::splat(cell_spacing);
48:         centre.x.abs() > interior.x || centre.y.abs() > interior.y
49:     }
50: 
51:     fn coverage(&self, centre: ScenePlanPoint) -> u8 {
52:         // The playable sward owns everything inside its rectangle. Gating per
53:         // tuft rather than per cell keeps the boundary exact, so neither
54:         // sward doubles up nor leaves a gap along it.
55:         if centre.metres().x.abs() <= self.playable_half_extent.x
56:             && centre.metres().y.abs() <= self.playable_half_extent.y
57:         {
58:             return 0;
59:         }
60:         let coverage = stitched_vista_topology_coverage(
61:             self.lod,
62:             self.playable_half_extent,
63:             self.playable_ground,
64:             centre,
65:             self.urban_ground,
66:         );
67:         (coverage.clamp(0.0, 1.0) * 255.0) as u8
68:     }
69: 
70:     fn height(&self, centre: ScenePlanPoint) -> Option<SupportElevation> {
71:         if self.playable_terrain.property_surface().is_some() {
72:             let hit = self
73:                 .playable_terrain
74:                 .surface_below(SupportQuery::unbounded(centre))?;
75:             return (hit.normal.y >= MINIMUM_GRASS_SLOPE_NORMAL_Y).then_some(hit.elevation);
76:         }
77:         let local = self.lod.local_offset(centre).ok()?;
78:         let geometry = VistaVertexGeometry::sample(
79:             self.lod,
80:             self.coarser_lod,
81:             Some(self.playable_terrain),
82:             local,
83:             self.playable_half_extent,
84:             PositiveLength::from_metres(2.0).ok()?,
85:         )?;
86:         let tangent_x = geometry.east_tangent().metres();
87:         let tangent_z = geometry.north_tangent().metres();
88:         let normal = tangent_z.cross(tangent_x).normalize_or_zero();
89:         (normal.y >= MINIMUM_GRASS_SLOPE_NORMAL_Y).then_some(geometry.elevation())
90:     }
91: 
92:     fn community(&mut self, centre: ScenePlanPoint) -> GrassCommunity {
93:         let profile = sample_vista_environment(self.lod, centre)
94:             .map_or(self.profile, |sample| self.profile.localized(sample));
95:         self.communities.at(centre, profile)
96:     }
97: }
98: 
99: #[expect(
100:     clippy::too_many_arguments,
101:     reason = "this domain boundary names each independent input explicitly"
102: )]
103: pub(super) fn spawn_near_vista_scatter(
104:     commands: &mut Commands,
105:     lod: &VistaLod,
106:     coarser_lod: Option<&VistaLod>,
107:     playable_half_extent: Vec2,
108:     playable_terrain: &SceneTerrain,
109:     playable_ground: &SceneGround,
110:     environment: &SceneEnvironment,
111:     meshes: &mut Assets<Mesh>,
112:     grass_materials: &mut Assets<TacticalGrassInstancedMaterial>,
113:     grass: &crate::presentation::config::GrassConfig,
114:     urban_ground: &UrbanGround,
115: ) {
116:     if !grass.enabled {
117:         return;
118:     }
119:     let scene_seed = stable_text_seed(&environment.scene_digest);
120:     let (grass_color, grass_dryness) = grass_pigment(environment);
121:     // Blade density has to match the playable sward exactly: the two lattices
122:     // abut along the playable rectangle, so any difference reads as a seam.
123:     let pigment = TuftPigment {
124:         color: grass_color,
125:         density: grass_scatter_density(
126:             bps(environment.canopy_bps),
127:             bps(environment.water_bps),
128:             bps(environment.cultivation_bps),
129:             bps(environment.weather.snow_cover_bps),
130:         ) * grass.density_scale,
131:         dryness: grass_dryness,
132:         wind_scale: 0.16 + bps(environment.weather.wind_speed_bps) * 0.36,
133:     };
134:     let grass_seed = streams::GRASS.seed(scene_seed, &[]);
135:     let mut batches = scatter(
136:         lod,
137:         coarser_lod,
138:         playable_half_extent,
139:         playable_terrain,
140:         playable_ground,
141:         environment,
142:         grass,
143:         urban_ground,
144:     );
145:     spawn_tuft_batches(
146:         GrassWorld {
147:             commands,
148:             meshes,
149:             materials: grass_materials,
150:         },
151:         &mut batches,
152:         "Vista grass",
153:         (VistaTerrain(lod.level), VistaGrassPresentation),
154:         grass_seed,
155:         pigment,
156:         grass,
157:     );
158: }
159: 
160: /// How far past the playable rectangle a ring tier scatters: its terminal fade
161: /// distance, since the camera never leaves the rectangle.
162: fn tier_sward_collar_metres(
163:     lod: GrassMeshLod,
164:     grass: &crate::presentation::config::GrassConfig,
165: ) -> f32 {
166:     let tier = match lod {
167:         GrassMeshLod::Near => &grass.lod.near,
168:         GrassMeshLod::NearEdge => &grass.lod.near_edge,
169:         GrassMeshLod::Far => &grass.lod.far,
170:         GrassMeshLod::Vista => &grass.lod.vista,
171:     };
172:     // The near tier hands off to near-edge, which reuses its placements, so the
173:     // near lattice has to reach as far as the wider of the two bands.
174:     tier.fade_out_m[1].max(grass.lod.near_edge.fade_out_m[1])
175: }
176: 
177: #[expect(
178:     clippy::too_many_arguments,
179:     reason = "Shared pure scatter inputs mirror the native rendering boundary"
180: )]
181: fn scatter(
182:     lod: &VistaLod,
183:     coarser_lod: Option<&VistaLod>,
184:     playable_half_extent: Vec2,
185:     playable_terrain: &SceneTerrain,
186:     playable_ground: &SceneGround,
187:     environment: &SceneEnvironment,
188:     grass: &crate::presentation::config::GrassConfig,
189:     urban_ground: &UrbanGround,
190: ) -> TierSpeciesBatches {
191:     if !grass.enabled {
192:         return Default::default();
193:     }
194:     let grass_seed = streams::GRASS.seed(stable_text_seed(&environment.scene_digest), &[]);
195:     let profile = GrassCommunityProfile::from_environment(environment);
196:     let placement = |outer_collar| VistaTuftPlacement {
197:         lod,
198:         coarser_lod,
199:         playable_half_extent,
200:         playable_terrain,
201:         playable_ground,
202:         urban_ground,
203:         profile,
204:         communities: GrassCommunityField::new(grass_seed),
205:         outer_collar,
206:     };
207: 
208:     // The playable boundary selects the height/cover data source, never the
209:     // representation. The same globally aligned lattice and distance ranges
210:     // continue across it, so crossing the boundary cannot introduce an LOD
211:     // edge or replace blank space with a close representation.
212:     //
213:     // Each tier only reaches as far as its own fade-out: the camera stays
214:     // inside the playable rectangle, so a tuft farther out than the tier's
215:     // terminal fade distance can never be drawn, and placing one would only
216:     // cost instance memory and compute-cull work.
217:     let mut batches = TierSpeciesBatches::default();
218:     for grass_lod in [GrassMeshLod::Near, GrassMeshLod::Far] {
219:         scatter_cell_tufts(
220:             &mut batches[grass_lod.tier_index()],
221:             &mut placement(tier_sward_collar_metres(grass_lod, grass)),
222:             grass_seed,
223:             grass_lod,
224:             grass.placement.playable_patch_spacing_m,
225:             grass,
226:         );
227:     }
228:     // Reuse the near placements, exactly as the playable sward does, so the
229:     // near-edge crossfade morphs each tuft in place instead of moving it.
230:     for species in GrassSpecies::ALL {
231:         batches[GrassMeshLod::NearEdge.tier_index()][species.index()] =
232:             batches[GrassMeshLod::Near.tier_index()][species.index()].clone();
233:     }
234:     scatter_cell_tufts(
235:         &mut batches[GrassMeshLod::Vista.tier_index()],
236:         &mut placement(tier_sward_collar_metres(GrassMeshLod::Vista, grass)),
237:         streams::GRASS_LOD.seed(grass_seed, &[]),
238:         GrassMeshLod::Vista,
239:         grass.placement.vista_patch_spacing_m,
240:         grass,
241:     );
242: 
243:     batches

357:     use std::{fs, path::Path};
358: 
359:     /// WGSL requires every directive to precede the first declaration, and an
360:     /// `#import` expands into declarations. A directive written below the
361:     /// imports fails composition for the whole file, which surfaces only as a
362:     /// log line while the material stops rendering on every backend.
363:     #[test]
364:     fn shader_directives_precede_declarations() {
365:         // Both shader roots the tactical renderer composes: the runtime asset
366:         // directory and the shaders embedded in the procedural materials crate.
367:         const SHADER_ROOTS: [&str; 2] = [
368:             concat!(env!("CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR"), "/../../assets/shaders"),
369:             concat!(
370:                 env!("CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR"),
371:                 "/../adventuresim-procedural-materials/src/shaders"
372:             ),
373:         ];
374:         let mut checked = 0;
375:         for root in SHADER_ROOTS {
376:             for entry in fs::read_dir(Path::new(root)).expect("tactical shader directory") {
377:                 let path = entry.expect("shader directory entry").path();
378:                 if path.extension().is_none_or(|extension| extension != "wgsl") {
379:                     continue;
380:                 }
381:                 let source = fs::read_to_string(&path).expect("readable tactical shader");
382:                 assert_directives_precede_declarations(&path.display().to_string(), &source);
383:                 checked += 1;
384:             }
385:         }
386:         assert!(checked > 0, "no tactical shaders were checked");
387:     }
388: 
389:     fn assert_directives_precede_declarations(label: &str, source: &str) {
390:         let mut declared = false;
391:         for (index, line) in source.lines().enumerate() {
392:             let line = line.trim();
393:             if line.is_empty() || line.starts_with("//") {
394:                 continue;
395:             }
396:             if line.starts_with("diagnostic(")
397:                 || line.starts_with("enable ")
398:                 || line.starts_with("requires ")
399:             {
400:                 assert!(
401:                     !declared,
402:                     "{label}:{}: WGSL directive written after a declaration; \
403:                      move it above the imports or the shader will not compile",
404:                     index + 1
405:                 );
406:             } else if !line.starts_with('#') || line.starts_with("#import") {
407:                 declared = true;
408:             }
409:         }
410:     }
411: }

112:     items: Query<Entity, With<super::equipment::SceneEquipment>>,
113:     mut settled: Local<usize>,
114:     (mut assets_ready, mut installed_ready): (
115:         ResMut<SceneAssetsReady>,
116:         ResMut<SceneInstallationReady>,
117:     ),
118:     cache: Res<super::cached_views::CachedViews>,
119:     city: Option<Res<crate::presentation::PendingCityBuildings>>,
120:     terrain: Query<(), With<crate::presentation::PendingTerrainPresentation>>,
121:     sky: Res<crate::presentation::AtmosphereIblCache>,
122:     settings: Res<crate::presentation::TacticalGraphicsSettings>,
123:     lighting: super::lighting_diagnostics::LightingDiagnostics,
124: ) {
125:     let waiting = waiting_pipelines();
126:     let equipment_state = equipment.check(items.iter());
127:     let equipment_ready = equipment_state == Ok(true);
128:     let counts = characters.counts(view.as_deref(), &scene);
129:     let textures_ready =
130:         textures.is_ready(PROCEDURAL_TEXTURE_CATALOGUE.iter().map(|recipe| recipe.id));
131:     if view.as_ref().is_some_and(|view| view.is_changed()) {
132:         *settled = 0;
133:     }
134:     let installed = view.as_ref().is_some_and(|view| {
135:         scene.location == view.location
136:             && scene.next_place == view.places.len()
137:             && scene.pending.is_empty()
138:             && view
139:                 .people
140:                 .iter()
141:                 .filter(|person| view.requires_person(person.id))
142:                 .all(|person| scene.people.contains_key(&person.id))
143:     }) && counts.loaded == scene.people.len()
144:         && counts.posed == counts.loaded
145:         && textures_ready
146:         && city.as_ref().is_none_or(|city| city.finished())
147:         && terrain.is_empty()
148:         && sky.is_ready(&settings)
149:         && failure.0.is_none()
150:         && scene.error.is_none();
151:     installed_ready.0 = installed;
152:     let complete = installed
153:         && equipment_ready
154:         && waiting == 0
155:         && city.as_ref().is_none_or(|city| {
156:             city.total == 0 || crate::presentation::city_gpu_ready(PresentationOwner::Scene)
157:         });
158:     assets_ready.0 = complete;
159:     if complete && cache.is_ready() {
160:         *settled += 1;
161:     } else {
162:         *settled = 0;
163:     }
164:     let status = Status {
165:         daylight: lighting.gpu.daylight(),
166:         view_lighting: lighting.views(),
167:         revision: view.as_ref().map_or(0, |view| view.revision),
168:         ready: *settled >= SETTLED_RENDER_FRAMES,
169:         assets_ready: complete,
170:         installed_ready: installed,
171:         snapshots_pending: cache.pending_captures(),
172:         settled_render_frames: *settled,
173:         buildings: scene.next_place,
174:         street: scene.street.clone(),
175:         characters: counts.roster,
176:         loaded_characters: counts.loaded,
177:         posed_characters: counts.posed,
178:         required_characters: counts.required,
179:         posed_required_characters: counts.required_posed,
180:         textures_ready,
181:         sky_ready: sky.is_ready(&settings),
182:         terrain_pending: terrain.iter().count(),
183:         city_pending: city
184:             .as_ref()
185:             .map_or(0, |city| city.total - city.completed()),
186:         waiting_pipelines: waiting,
187:         equipment_ready,
188:         equipment_pending: (!equipment_ready).then(|| equipment.pending_summary(items.iter())),
189:         error: status_error(&scene, &failure, city.as_deref(), equipment_state),
190:     };
191:     status.publish();
192: }
193: 
194: fn status_error(
195:     scene: &RetainedScene,
196:     failure: &SceneAssetFailure,
197:     city: Option<&crate::presentation::PendingCityBuildings>,
198:     equipment_state: std::result::Result<bool, &'static str>,
199: ) -> Option<String> {
200:     scene
201:         .error
202:         .as_ref()
203:         .map(ToString::to_string)
204:         .or_else(|| failure.0.clone())
205:         .or_else(|| city.and_then(|city| city.failure().map(str::to_owned)))
206:         .or_else(|| equipment_state.err().map(str::to_owned))
207: }

# Fabelgeist tactical client

[Immutable scene preparation](generation.md) describes shared worker products,
readiness, residency and typed preparation failures.

[Regional environment presentation](regional-map.md) describes the retained
geographic camera, terrain surface and browser command boundary.

The atmosphere extraction backport is required by the selected Bevy 0.19 engine.
The build script reads the resolved version from the workspace lockfile and
requires removing that backport and its guard when the project selects Bevy 0.20
or later. Releasing a new upstream engine does not change the selected engine or
make an otherwise unchanged build fail. This check does not access the network.

## Runtime equipment fitting

Armor and clothing are generated locally from each wearer's evaluated, unposed
body. Identity and skeletal fit morphs are evaluated on the body once; skeletal
proportion offsets then place its vertices and fitting landmarks. Equipment
contains no body-shape morph targets. Its inverse bind poses belong to that
wearer's rest skeleton, so animation does not apply proportion changes twice.

The client queues fitting outside frame updates on native builds and awaits
WebGPU initialization and readback in the browser. The compute device creates
no canvas; Bevy renders the resulting geometry in the existing game canvas.
Offline exporters retain their reusable morph-equipped asset workflow.
Compute and rendering dependencies must use the same `wgpu` release: linking
two releases into the browser client duplicates their vendored WebGPU bindings.

Strategic loading fits the equipment actually requested by the scene. The device
and compiled compute kernels stay alive across city travel; loading does not fit
and discard the entire authored catalog first. Strategic scene readiness waits
for its requested fits, and preparation failures surface as loading errors.
Newly encountered wearers receive their own fitted meshes.

Fits are cached by item design, anatomical placement, and evaluated body shape.
The last 128 variants remain available across travel; live entities retain their
own mesh handles after cache eviction. Changing wearer or proportions requests a
new fit. Holding or dropping a previously fitted item preserves its shape and
anatomical placement across placeholder rebuilds. Carried and dropped meshes
are centered rigid objects; only worn equipment binds to the wearer's skeleton.

Measure fitting separately from rendering with the real canonical body:

```powershell
cargo run -p adventuresim-tactical-client --example runtime_equipment_bench -- assets/animations/biped/unarmed/base.glb 3
```

The JSON records separate device opening, first use, and repeated fits. The
vambrace and breastplate comparisons use the same batched readback for one body
and the full set of body morph endpoints; they isolate morph generation cost.
The browser probe example exercises the same asynchronous runtime generator.
Build it with `cargo build -p adventuresim-tactical-client --example
armor_browser_probe --target wasm32-unknown-unknown --no-default-features`.
Run the matching `wasm-bindgen` CLI with `--target web` into an output directory,
copy `examples/armor_browser_probe.html` there as `index.html`, and copy
`assets/animations/biped/unarmed/base.glb` from the repository as `body.glb`.
Serve that directory on localhost. The page reports initial preparation time,
geometry validity, and first and repeated fitting times for twelve equipment
types after preparation. Kernel counts identify any missed first-use work.
Gorget and mail-coif section measurements intersect body triangles, so fitting
does not require dense vertices near each anatomical measurement plane.

`animation-viewer --armor-harness wearer-fit` renders a gorget, cuirass, and
paired vambraces on the actual animated wearer for fitting inspection.
Device builders generate pauldrons, wrapped tassets, anime breastplates, and
puff-and-slash clothing as well. Unsupported recipes fail readiness instead of
loading served equipment meshes or silently substituting another design.

Generated equipment uses ordinary skeletal attachment during animation. Metal
parts retain their authored rigid joint ownership; cuirass courses share one
chest attachment, and pauldron distal lames follow the upper arm. There is no
runtime plate solver, body collision mesh, or per-frame contact search in this
generation path. Generation-time layer fitting and closed-shell validation do
not establish collision-free animation. Independent plate articulation and
contact correction are separate work.

## Browser release builds

`just build-wasm` keeps the gameplay client on the workspace `release` profile
and builds the art demo separately with the size-oriented `wasm-release`
profile and no default features. The demo therefore excludes client audio and
debug tooling without removing either from ordinary client builds. The build
requires the exact `wasm-bindgen` version in `Cargo.lock` and the Binaryen
version pinned in the root `package-lock.json`; run `npm ci` to install the
latter.

The build applies `wasm-opt -Oz` only to the art demo after `wasm-bindgen` and
writes raw, gzip level 6, and Brotli level 11 sizes to
`crates/adventuresim-stdb-module/static/wasm/bundle-sizes.json`. In the browser,
the developer console's `[art-demo startup]` record separates module download
from Wasm compilation and initialization, making a cold-cache startup directly
repeatable in browser developer tools.

Outdoor PBR lighting uses Bevy's live atmosphere for sunlight transmission,
horizon occlusion, the solar disc and aerial perspective. Generated sky
radiance supplies diffuse and specular environment lighting at intensity one;
there is no added global ambient visibility floor. The environment map is
cached only after GPU completion and invalidated by scene, weather, time,
selected atmosphere, its position/scale, or scattering-medium changes. Camera
exposure does not invalidate unexposed sky radiance. Probe retirement runs
after Bevy's deferred preparation commands. The live atmosphere remains enabled
after the environment bake.

The pinned Bevy 0.19.1 atmosphere shaders use local, source-attributed
corrections: generation samples texel centres, and the forward/inverse lookup
coordinate maps agree. Canonical shader handles and imports stay intact, so
visible sky and environment baking use the same mapping. A shader reload
invalidates the bake; capture readiness waits for the corrected GPU pipelines.
The analytic planet ground samples sunlight transmission at its surface
radius, retaining the dependence on solar angle.
With multisample anti-aliasing, atmospheric scattering and transmission use
each sample's depth and viewport position, so mixed terrain/sky pixels receive
the corresponding transport before color resolution.

This environment map samples the atmospheric medium; the separate animated
cloud renderer is not included in it. Cloud radiance, cloud beam transmission,
and scene bounce lighting require further transport integration. The existing
weather source attenuation is an approximation, not a full cloud-scattering
solution.

The tactical client renders transient server-authoritative combat state with
Bevy. Skeletal animation is presentation-only: the server replicates compact
`SkeletonState` posture, locomotion, stance, action, and timing coordinates;
the client selects and blends authored poses, then applies procedural look and
terrain leg IK.

The equipment HUD shows procedural weapons, holders, and armor as color
portraits on black squares. Weapon recipes render into a transient image cache;
armor loads the baked portrait for its manifest placement. See the
[portrait workflow](../adventuresim-weapon-model/README.md#equipment-portraits)
for lighting and regeneration commands.

EGUI renders the centered incapacitation wheel without taking pointer input.
The segmented arc surrounds the retained Bevy UI crosshair, starts at 12
o'clock, and uses the strategic condition colors for live pain and blood loss
plus enrolled fear, fatigue, hunger, thirst, and temperature; tactical
imbalance is white. Zero incapacitation draws nothing and a full revolution is
the visible maximum.

The gameplay camera is likewise client presentation. A single retained rig
blends from centered lowered-guard exploration to raised-guard right-shoulder
aiming without smoothing manual yaw or pitch. Focus translation uses bounded
anisotropic critical damping and a screen-space sweet spot sized to the current
boom distance. A box enclosing the eye and near-plane corners sweeps from the
controller center around hard geometry. The final framed position is swept
again, so shoulder offsets and focus lag cannot bypass the collision check.
Tight spaces blend toward a close shoulder view with a small height offset and
reduced focus lag. Collision and close framing are resolved together before
recovery, including corners where the close view meets a second obstacle.

Retraction is immediate; recovery waits briefly and then uses critical damping
and distance hysteresis. Soft occluders remain excluded from camera collision.
Raised aiming resolves the center-screen camera target and the subsequent
muzzle path separately. Debug builds use `F6` to show rig, collision, smoothing,
occlusion classification, and aim-ray telemetry.

Camera frame intervals are capped at 0.1 seconds. Collision hold time is a
finite nonnegative interval, including zero, with the existing 0.12-second
default. Horizontal and vertical follow, mode-transition and collision-recovery
coefficients are finite signed shaping seconds. Profile interpolation precedes
the damping equation's existing response floor, so finite zero and negative
coefficients retain their behavior. Invalid authored temporal values fail
checked admission. Blend and profile results are prepared before replacing
their retained filter values; this does not make all camera updates atomic.

The tactical workspace targets Bevy 0.19, Avian 0.7, Ahoy 0.2, Replicon
0.41, Aeronet 0.21, Enhanced Input 0.26, and Flair 0.8. The engine upgrade does
not move animation or movement authority: `SkeletonState` and controller state
remain server-owned, while authored pose evaluation, lighting, and the Bevy
world-asset scene attachment are client presentation. Native and Wasm builds
share those semantics through their existing explicit feature sets.

## Client-generated geological geometry

Collider-bearing rocks replicate compact recipes containing a seed, silhouette
archetype, lithology, dimensions, and conservative collision radius. The
tactical server creates only the bounded sphere collider and transform. The
client samples each recipe on a small uniform grid and extracts its render
surface with the private Surface Nets implementation in
`src/presentation/volumetric.rs`; it rejects non-finite fields and tests the
result for deterministic, outward, closed topology. Loose-stone ground cover
reuses four shared client-generated variants without collision or foliage wind.

This extractor is infrastructure for later bounded cliffs, overhangs, and cave
patches, not an implemented cave system. Future scene authority must send a
compact deterministic field recipe, never a server-generated render mesh.
Authored clips are sampled by the client-owned pose buffer. The semantic router
reads presentation state, resolves weighted clip samples through the animation
pack catalog, and applies fixed-rate FK with per-joint inertialization before
procedural terrain, body-response, and weapon-constraint passes. The validated
server configuration owns each sampling rate and its positive reciprocal.
Buffered sample counts are distinct from elapsed seconds and absolute ticks;
checked interval arithmetic precedes replacement of buffered poses. Inertial
clocks retain checked elapsed time while their polynomial kernels keep the
existing numerical stencil and denominator floors.
Pose buffers distinguish inactive state from retained authored display history.
The first plan snaps to its target; later transitions capture displayed output.
Visibility and physics ownership remain separate: pinning a physics pose does
not establish authored display history. Ordinary locomotion adopts its first
vertical hip correction even at zero elapsed time, then retains that correction
on subsequent zero-elapsed observations.

Shared semantic evaluation and resolved playback carry the same core
`BlendWeight`, `CyclePhase` and `ClipMirror` owners. Weights admit every finite
nonnegative contribution, including values above one; checked accumulation
rejects overflow. Cycles remain finite, signed and unwrapped until a periodic
operation. Mirroring remains binary and serializes as a Boolean. Declared span
endpoints remain in the playback plan even at zero weight; numerical sampling
skips zero contributions. Continuation coordinates and their tangent operations
remain distinct from cyclic phase.

`ClipDuration` admits finite nonnegative seconds, while `ClipTime` admits signed
finite sample positions. Baked clips and both span families retain checked times
and weights until native interpolation or Bevy sampling. Pose interpolation
carries a checked fraction of the fixed sample interval.

The deterministic override stores an `AnimationSampleTick` with the shared
`AnimationElapsed` interval. Repeated observations retain zero elapsed time.
Body response carries finite signed angles, angular velocities and body-local

nonnegative metre distances; absorption/recovery use nonnegative metre-per-second

Combat YAML owns the observation cap, calibration grid and accepted foot range,

Cadence retains checked nonnegative step distances and stance-slip budgets;
selected-axis calibration positions retain signed metres. A fitted phase curve
owns its periodic sample grid and checked seam; an empty or singleton mapping
is explicitly identity, while missing calibration remains absent. Each motion

Capture plans and required cadence acceptance propagate distance failures before

Height amplitudes and speeds share zero-permitting finite measurement leaves.
Body angles retain their signed response-frame role; angular caps use a finite

## Animation export contract

The humanoid base rig is independent from authored motions:

```text
assets/animations/biped/unarmed/walk.glb
assets/animations/biped/unarmed/swing.glb

assets/animations/biped/unarmed/offhand.glb
```

Only `base.glb` supplies a spawnable scene. Its default scene must retain the

other file contains exactly one coherent motion, named or unnamed, and never

file/frame anchor and includes unnamed endpoint/closure frames. Source motion

rig-source special case until `assets_src/biped/unarmed/base.casc` has a
matching
base GLB export.

Publish and verify every currently available runtime animation without changing
source exports:

```powershell
python scripts/prepare_rig_base.py assets_src/biped/unarmed/base.glb assets/animations/biped/unarmed/base.glb
python scripts/prepare_animation_assets.py
python scripts/prepare_animation_assets.py --check
```

Motion publication validates the one-animation, duration, and canonical
bone-path contracts. Runtime motion GLBs preserve only the canonical hierarchy,
bind transforms, and animation data; mesh, skin, material, texture, and image

only catalog-addressable frames for ordinary motions, removes tracks that equal
the bind transform, and collapses other constant tracks to one key. Walk and run
store five cubic anchor keys rather than Cascadeur's exported in-betweens.
The `.casc` projects are tracked authoring sources. Their reproducible
`assets_src/**/*.glb` exports are ignored; export them locally before publishing
the tracked runtime GLBs.

Use these conventions:

- glTF coordinates and meters: +Y up, -Z forward, +X anatomical left;
- the scene root stays at the origin and gameplay movement is not baked into it;
- the armature bind pose is a T-pose, which is the final runtime fallback;
- each motion GLB contains exactly one animation and preserves its documented
  semantic anchors;
- locomotion uses only its contact and passing/flight anchor frames. The
  runtime constructs contact -> passing -> mirrored contact -> mirrored
  passing -> contact by sampling the two exact catalog frames on distinct Bevy

Lower-body reflection is evaluated in character space so anatomical left and
right retain their lateral spacing while exchanging gait roles. Authored
upper-body carriage remains intact; explicit hand targets and weapon
constraints apply only when gameplay supplies them. Root, pelvis, spine, neck,
and head translations are clamped around the authored bind pose before look
and final IK, while authored joint rotations remain intact. During active
locomotion, sparse anchor blending advances linearly with phase so the pose
cannot ease to a hold and then accelerate between anchors. Gait parity is
binary per endpoint and is applied before blending; the runtime never
fractionally reflects an already blended skeleton, which would collapse the
forward/back separation of bilateral limbs.
Authored root/pelvis Y is normalized, then the

arc with two phase-aligned peaks per cycle without moving the gameplay
controller. A contact-edge calibration translates the complete visual rig so
the supported sole meets the rig floor, then retains that baseline through the
stride without reconstructing either leg. Idle poses blend back
to their authored central-bone transforms. The 33mm hierarchy compensation is
measured for upright, lowered-guard `humanoid_unarmed` locomotion only; guard
movement and specialized packs receive no inferred compensation.

## Deterministic animation capture

Republish after changing any motion with
`python scripts/prepare_animation_assets.py`; CI-style verification uses the
same command with `--check`. The publisher requires Python 3 and NumPy.

The native `animation-viewer` binary is a deterministic gameplay-presentation
fixture rather than a separate pose renderer. It installs the gameplay player,
camera, scene presentation, authored FK, pre-mirrored gait endpoints, whole-body
fallback mirroring, look, and terrain-IK plugins, then advances the shared
authoritative locomotion projector at its real 64Hz fixed tick. Default-off
scenarios retain authored ordinary leg motion with a vertically fixed gameplay
root; the explicit cross-slope scenario opts into the seeded terrain-IK pass.
Coverage includes two-cycle 2.0m/s walk, 3.75m/s blend, 5.5m/s run, raised-guard
full/half-speed movement, and start/stop, guard-entry, and guard-release
transitions. Every logical tick is captured first from the raw gameplay
third-person camera, then from side and front diagnostic cameras with a skeleton
overlay and yellow supported-foot / pink swing-foot markers. The simulation is
frozen while those three views are rendered, so they describe one pose. The
output includes per-view PNG sequences, `manifest.json` bone and support
telemetry, and an `index.html` normal/half/quarter-speed reviewer with
representative contact sheets. A missing rig or unresolved locomotion clip times
out with `failure.txt` rather than hanging.

Run it from the repository root:

```powershell
cargo run -p adventuresim-tactical-client --bin animation-viewer -- --output target/animation-captures/locomotion-review
```

Use `--armor-harness close-helmet` to generate the close helmet through
normal gameplay equipment loading. Capture waits for fitted geometry,
materials, wearer skin bindings, and the absence of equipment morph targets.
Front and side views follow the head at inspection distance; the
gameplay view keeps its usual framing. `armor-readiness.json` records the
resolved parts and weights. `--scenario ordinary-camera-pitch` exercises
lowered-guard idle and head pitch; `--scenario raised-guard-stationary-turn`
exercises guard and turning. Add `--hidden` for automated captures without a
visible desktop window.

For supplementary boundary inspection, use `--camera-orbit-degrees 120` to
rotate the front and side cameras around their existing focus. Gameplay framing
stays unchanged. `--diffuse-armor` removes metallic highlights and makes the
supporting cuirass translucent while keeping body anatomy visible. The capture
records these options in `inspection.json`; neither option changes fitting.

Use `--armor-harness puffed` for paired puff-and-slash sleeves and hose. Their
ring and panel geometry, anatomical section fitting, shell extrusion, and skin
correspondence run on the client GPU. Component materials retain the authored
outer fabric and undercloth colors. Worn parts share the evaluated wearer rig;
carried or dropped material parts retain one common item origin.

Use `--asset-root` when invoking it outside the repository root,
`--scenario steady-walk-2.0` for a focused iteration, and
`--frames-per-sample` to change the render settle interval (not the simulated
64Hz sample interval). Open `index.html` after capture and review each scenario
at normal speed before using slow motion. The manifest tracks pelvis, chest,
head, shoulders, elbows, hands, hips, knees, and feet; finite transforms; loop
seams; per-frame displacement and rotation spikes; knee direction;
terrain-relative foot clearance/support/slip; contact-sole grounding;
controller-height stability;
phase-indexed contact/pass height; visual peak count; run flight duration and
sole clearance; and pelvis/head stability. These
values are regression signals and do not establish biomechanical correctness
without visual review.
Capture fails for teleport-scale continuity, ground penetration, duplicate
front/side/third-person image output, missing artifacts, or excessive
supported-foot per-frame slip and planted-interval drift, and records the
responsible frames.

The fixture synthesizes deterministic controller observations at the shared
server projection boundary; it does not run the transport or physics character
controller. Only the cross-slope probe follows rendered
terrain height; flat scenarios verify that animation never changes controller Y.

Use the supervised diagnostic profile when a problem appears in gameplay but
not in `animation-viewer`:

```powershell
just tactical-play diagnostic
```

This launches the ordinary native client, server, transport, replicated
physics controller, and rendering stack. Once the controlled character is
available, the client turns 90 degrees right, holds forward at 0.5 analogue

The procedural humanoid pass recognizes these case-sensitive bone names:

```text
body_world           root                 c_spine0 / c_spine1
c_spine2 / c_spine3  c_neck               c_head / c_camera
l_clavicle / r_clavicle                   l_uparm / r_uparm
l_lowarm / r_lowarm  l_wrist / r_wrist    l_weapon / r_weapon
l_upleg / r_upleg    l_lowleg / r_lowleg  l_foot / r_foot
l_ball / r_ball
```

Procedural binding and pelvis masks use the same exact bone roles: `root` is
the pelvis and `body_world` is the rig root. Other spellings, including
`ROOT` and `Root`, remain unbound and receive no special pelvis masking or
terrain-reference treatment. Topology rebuilds preserve the calibrated left
and right sole axes; each axis is captured once from the authored bind pose.

Finger, face, foot-articulation, and distributed twist bones retain authored FK.
They still participate in full-pose mirroring. `l_weapon`, `r_weapon`, and
`c_camera` are export-added attachment joints on the canonical MHR hierarchy.
Equipment removes each target's rolled authored bind frame before following its
live deformation; worn placeholders derive their +Y axis from semantic joint
pairs, while held weapons retain the character-space +Y tip convention.

The final client-only pose pass distributes bounded look across the actual
spine/neck chain, converts bounded pelvis compensation through its real parent,
and solves legs and optional hand targets across the MHR hierarchy without
overwriting authored twist locals. Foot slope alignment uses the authored bind
transform to derive its sole-up axis rather than assuming an MHR joint-local
cardinal axis. A primary hand socket drives a held weapon, then an optional
weapon-local secondary grip drives the off hand. These targets and constraints
are client-only and never extend replicated `SkeletonState`.

## Missing assets

Ordinary pose lookup first follows the pack's single fallback chain, then its
deterministic similar-pose chain. Attack availability is stricter because it is
a gameplay capability. A pack that defines `swing` or `thrust` owns that
complete main-hand set, and an absent family stays unavailable; only a pack
with neither motion inherits its parent's main-hand attacks. `offhand` resolves
independently through the parent chain. Missing, unloaded, zero-animation,
multiple-animation, or short motion files are unavailable.
Absent optional motion files are logged at info level while pose lookup uses
the available fallbacks, including mirrored poses. Other loading failures
remain errors, and invalid motion contents retain their validation warnings.
Every local or remote character also gets a generated T-pose safety net until
the base scene is available. Bind locals are reset before every animation
evaluation so partial clips cannot accumulate stale or procedural transforms.

## City ground and outdoor furniture

City streets and developed yards use one production material policy across
playable and distant ground. Metre-space cobble and gravel detail blends with
compacted earth, broken edges, static traffic wear, and weather-dependent
dampness. Accepted vendor, receiving, and horse-stop footprints contribute
local wear masks. Static traffic history adds seven carriage gauges, lateral
variation, and tangent-continuous turns at shared endpoints and interior
crossings. Turning front and rear axles leave overlapping marks in both travel
directions, constrained to the visible road/market union. Broad churn covers
most of the central carriageway; wheel marks break up within those deposits.

Traffic, churn, and road-union shoulders are baked once into 64-metre tiles at
four texels per metre. Neighboring tiles share world-space filter gutters, and
all overlapping ground patches sample the same masks. Ground meshes split at
tile boundaries while retaining canonical terrain support. The furniture capture
gate checks the ground masks are GPU resident, and its junction views show
turning continuity and axle variation. Ground meshes sample the same presented
terrain surface; material relief does not change tactical collision or create
physical ruts.

Vista construction shades each environmental sample once for its exact weather
snapshot, then interpolates those linear colours across terrain vertices and
LOD seams. The temporary sample fields stay local to one ring construction and
follow the scene sample bounds. Geometry, colour interpolation order, substrate
pigments and distant sward coverage remain unchanged. Playable-edge pigment is
prepared once with the same scene environment.

Whole foundations are selected conservatively against each ring’s output
rectangles before internal sides are matched. Their bounds include closed-cell
vertices and exposed cut faces. Every intersecting property retains its
original face order and exact clipping; the physical support and collision
representation remain complete. Selection stays local to preparation.

The vista partitioner scans ordered accepted faces once per ring and prepares
each face's rectangle bounds once. Per-rectangle buffers retain source triangle
order; complete chunks retain clipping, normals, pigments and mesh indices.
These buffers contain only current mesh output and are released after
preparation. They do not retain another terrain or collision representation.

Operable windows retain checked scene positions/directions and positive leaf
dimensions through installation and presentation. The closure mesh cache accepts
`LeafDimensions` and converts to the cuboid mesh contract at its explicit native
cache/mesh adapter. Fixed glazing still admits thin or degenerate cuboid geometry.
Cache keys, shared handles and material selection keep their native layouts.
Core's paired `SceneWindowPose` supplies the converted leaf and native rotation.
Building closure visibility and shutter lighting carry `SceneBuildingId` and
`OpeningAssemblyId` through their joins. Material palette selection extracts the
native building number only at the existing deterministic seed/hash adapter.
Fixed bar presence uses the named `WindowBarPresence` enum in both scene APIs
and the serialized `bars` field.

Window animation and catch decisions remain transient server state. The mutable
controller's current angle and ordinary toggle `bool` are a documented #770
handoff under #765; distinguishing controller missing/blocked outcomes is outside
the selected #794 geometry change. Generator admission belongs to #766 and the
shared architectural-to-scene conversion belongs to #767.

Outdoor furniture arrives as compact immutable recipe references and normal
entity transforms. Shared mesh handles and the building material palette
render each accepted instance. Small furniture fades over 180-230 metres;
canvas stalls remain visible to 350-450 metres. Market and frontage placement
extends through the nearest vista ring. Distant furniture shares the production
recipe renderer but receives no physics or ordinary entity replication.
The core owns the clipped vista cells and vertex-height policy used by both
placement and terrain rendering, including seams and LOD morphs.
`python scripts/capture_furniture_review.py --output target/furniture-review`
captures the production implementation with GPU residency and material checks.

## Art-demo cloud assets

The fixed city and oak exhibits embed deterministic initial cloud-shell bakes,
so selecting either exhibit performs no procedural cloud bake on the browser
main thread. Each bake has a generated `.scene-digest` identity; the exhibit
refuses stale output rather than silently baking during navigation. Regenerate
and verify both assets after changing cloud bake logic or either tactical-scene
fixture:

```sh
cargo test -p adventuresim-tactical-client --bin art-demo \
  regenerate_art_demo_cloud_assets -- --ignored --nocapture
```

Production tactical scenes do not use these assets and retain runtime cloud
animation.

## Terrain comparison captures

The `terrain-grounding` capture profile requires explicit frozen world-space
cameras through `--city-cameras`. It renders at 2240 × 1260 physical pixels,
independent of desktop scaling. The image manifest reports those same physical
dimensions. Other capture profiles retain their standard 1280 × 720 images;
scene-performance measurements use a separate 2560 × 1440 offscreen target.
Cameras, time, weather, exposure and physical member selection must be fixed
when comparing terrain support across generated products and building LODs.
Explicit capture members are prepared for playable presentation only after the
unchanged input has reconstructed its accepted terrain. Their exact programmes,
placements and floor elevations are retained, and their distant drawing entries
are suppressed. The existing authoritative projectors generate each selected
owner's enclosure and garden against that same accepted terrain. The saved
input and scene digest identify the authoritative
source; `fixed-camera-contract.json` records this presentation selection.
Ordinary images and wireframe/collision diagnostics are separate evidence.

# Fabelgeist tactical client

[Immutable scene preparation](generation.md) describes shared worker products,
readiness, residency and typed preparation failures.

[Regional environment presentation](regional-map.md) describes the retained
geographic camera, terrain surface and browser command boundary.

The atmosphere extraction backport is required by the selected Bevy 0.19 engine.
The build script reads the resolved version from the workspace lockfile and
requires removing that backport and its guard when the project selects Bevy 0.20
or later. Releasing a new upstream engine does not change the selected engine or
make an otherwise unchanged build fail. This check does not access the network.

## Runtime equipment fitting

Armor and clothing are generated locally from each wearer's evaluated, unposed
body. Identity and skeletal fit morphs are evaluated on the body once; skeletal
proportion offsets then place its vertices and fitting landmarks. Equipment
contains no body-shape morph targets. Its inverse bind poses belong to that
wearer's rest skeleton, so animation does not apply proportion changes twice.

The client queues fitting outside frame updates on native builds and awaits
WebGPU initialization and readback in the browser. The compute device creates
no canvas; Bevy renders the resulting geometry in the existing game canvas.
Offline exporters retain their reusable morph-equipped asset workflow.
Compute and rendering dependencies must use the same `wgpu` release: linking
two releases into the browser client duplicates their vendored WebGPU bindings.

Strategic loading fits the equipment actually requested by the scene. The device
and compiled compute kernels stay alive across city travel; loading does not fit
and discard the entire authored catalog first. Strategic scene readiness waits
for its requested fits, and preparation failures surface as loading errors.
Newly encountered wearers receive their own fitted meshes.

Fits are cached by item design, anatomical placement, and evaluated body shape.
The last 128 variants remain available across travel; live entities retain their
own mesh handles after cache eviction. Changing wearer or proportions requests a
new fit. Holding or dropping a previously fitted item preserves its shape and
anatomical placement across placeholder rebuilds. Carried and dropped meshes
are centered rigid objects; only worn equipment binds to the wearer's skeleton.

Measure fitting separately from rendering with the real canonical body:

```powershell
cargo run -p adventuresim-tactical-client --example runtime_equipment_bench -- assets/animations/biped/unarmed/base.glb 3
```

The JSON records separate device opening, first use, and repeated fits. The
vambrace and breastplate comparisons use the same batched readback for one body
and the full set of body morph endpoints; they isolate morph generation cost.
The browser probe example exercises the same asynchronous runtime generator.
Build it with `cargo build -p adventuresim-tactical-client --example
armor_browser_probe --target wasm32-unknown-unknown --no-default-features`.
Run the matching `wasm-bindgen` CLI with `--target web` into an output directory,
copy `examples/armor_browser_probe.html` there as `index.html`, and copy
`assets/animations/biped/unarmed/base.glb` from the repository as `body.glb`.
Serve that directory on localhost. The page reports initial preparation time,
geometry validity, and first and repeated fitting times for twelve equipment
types after preparation. Kernel counts identify any missed first-use work.
Gorget and mail-coif section measurements intersect body triangles, so fitting
does not require dense vertices near each anatomical measurement plane.

`animation-viewer --armor-harness wearer-fit` renders a gorget, cuirass, and
paired vambraces on the actual animated wearer for fitting inspection.
Device builders generate pauldrons, wrapped tassets, anime breastplates, and
puff-and-slash clothing as well. Unsupported recipes fail readiness instead of
loading served equipment meshes or silently substituting another design.

Generated equipment uses ordinary skeletal attachment during animation. Metal
parts retain their authored rigid joint ownership; cuirass courses share one
chest attachment, and pauldron distal lames follow the upper arm. There is no
runtime plate solver, body collision mesh, or per-frame contact search in this
generation path. Generation-time layer fitting and closed-shell validation do
not establish collision-free animation. Independent plate articulation and
contact correction are separate work.

## Tactical loading screen

Spawning a tactical client, on native startup or browser `enter-tactical`,
starts a load. An opaque overlay with one progress bar per stage covers the
scene while it builds behind it, because render pipelines only compile for
what is actually drawn. Player input, cursor capture and the egui overlays stay
held until the reveal.

The stages are connection, joining the scene, textures, terrain, distant
landscape, trees, ground cover, sky, equipment, the local character's pose and
shaders. Each reads the marker left by the system doing that work. Trees and
shaders have no known total, so their largest observed backlog stands in for
one. Tree, vista and ground-cover generation run inside a single frame, so
those bars jump from empty to full while that frame blocks.

When every stage has been finished for four consecutive frames the overlay
fades out over 0.6 seconds. A load fails if the connection ends, a required
asset cannot be loaded, or no stage changes for 90 seconds of game time, which
stops while a browser tab is in the background. The equipment stage finishes
once generation has fitted or failed everything characters carry, so an item
that cannot be generated is logged and left out rather than ending the load.
Failure shows the reason with Retry, which spawns a new client for the same
server and character, and Exit, which quits the native client or calls the host
page's `window.exitTactical()` in the browser.

Pipelines first used after the reveal, such as those for objects outside the
initial view, can still compile during play. A connection lost after the reveal
keeps the HUD's existing "Disconnected" status. Headless clients run without
the screen, so automation controls input from the first frame.

## Browser release builds

`just build-wasm` keeps the gameplay client on the workspace `release` profile
and builds the art demo separately with the size-oriented `wasm-release`
profile and no default features. The demo therefore excludes client audio and
debug tooling without removing either from ordinary client builds. The build
requires the exact `wasm-bindgen` version in `Cargo.lock` and the Binaryen
version pinned in the root `package-lock.json`; run `npm ci` to install the
latter.

The build applies `wasm-opt -Oz` only to the art demo after `wasm-bindgen` and
writes raw, gzip level 6, and Brotli level 11 sizes to
`crates/adventuresim-stdb-module/static/wasm/bundle-sizes.json`. In the browser,
the developer console's `[art-demo startup]` record separates module download
from Wasm compilation and initialization, making a cold-cache startup directly
repeatable in browser developer tools.

Outdoor PBR lighting uses Bevy's live atmosphere for sunlight transmission,
horizon occlusion, the solar disc and aerial perspective. Generated sky
radiance supplies diffuse and specular environment lighting at intensity one;
there is no added global ambient visibility floor. The environment map is
cached only after GPU completion and invalidated by scene, weather, time,
selected atmosphere, its position/scale, or scattering-medium changes. Camera
exposure does not invalidate unexposed sky radiance. Probe retirement runs
after Bevy's deferred preparation commands. The live atmosphere remains enabled
after the environment bake.

The pinned Bevy 0.19.1 atmosphere shaders use local, source-attributed
corrections: generation samples texel centres, and the forward/inverse lookup
coordinate maps agree. Canonical shader handles and imports stay intact, so
visible sky and environment baking use the same mapping. A shader reload
invalidates the bake; capture readiness waits for the corrected GPU pipelines.
The analytic planet ground samples sunlight transmission at its surface
radius, retaining the dependence on solar angle.
With multisample anti-aliasing, atmospheric scattering and transmission use
each sample's depth and viewport position, so mixed terrain/sky pixels receive
the corresponding transport before color resolution.

This environment map samples the atmospheric medium; the separate animated
cloud renderer is not included in it. Cloud radiance, cloud beam transmission,
and scene bounce lighting require further transport integration. The existing
weather source attenuation is an approximation, not a full cloud-scattering
solution.

The tactical client renders transient server-authoritative combat state with
Bevy. Skeletal animation is presentation-only: the server replicates compact
`SkeletonState` posture, locomotion, stance, action, and timing coordinates;
the client selects and blends authored poses, then applies procedural look and
terrain leg IK.

The equipment HUD shows procedural weapons, holders, and armor as color
portraits on black squares. Weapon recipes render into a transient image cache;
armor loads the baked portrait for its manifest placement. See the

Tight spaces blend toward a close shoulder view with a small height offset and
reduced focus lag. Collision and close framing are resolved together before
recovery, including corners where the close view meets a second obstacle.
Retraction is immediate; recovery waits briefly and then uses critical damping
and distance hysteresis. Soft occluders remain excluded from camera collision.
Raised aiming resolves the center-screen camera target and the subsequent
muzzle path separately. Debug builds use `F6` to show rig, collision, smoothing,
occlusion classification, and aim-ray telemetry.

Camera frame intervals are capped at 0.1 seconds. Collision hold time is a
finite nonnegative interval, including zero, with the existing 0.12-second
default. Horizontal and vertical follow, mode-transition and collision-recovery
coefficients are finite signed shaping seconds. Profile interpolation precedes
the damping equation's existing response floor, so finite zero and negative
coefficients retain their behavior. Invalid authored temporal values fail
checked admission. Blend and profile results are prepared before replacing
their retained filter values; this does not make all camera updates atomic.

The tactical workspace targets Bevy 0.19, Avian 0.7, Ahoy 0.2, Replicon
0.41, Aeronet 0.21, Enhanced Input 0.26, and Flair 0.8. The engine upgrade does
not move animation or movement authority: `SkeletonState` and controller state
remain server-owned, while authored pose evaluation, lighting, and the Bevy
world-asset scene attachment are client presentation. Native and Wasm builds
share those semantics through their existing explicit feature sets.

## Client-generated geological geometry

Collider-bearing rocks replicate compact recipes containing a seed, silhouette
archetype, lithology, dimensions, and conservative collision radius. The
tactical server creates only the bounded sphere collider and transform. The
client samples each recipe on a small uniform grid and extracts its render
surface with the private Surface Nets implementation in
`src/presentation/volumetric.rs`; it rejects non-finite fields and tests the
result for deterministic, outward, closed topology. Loose-stone ground cover
reuses four shared client-generated variants without collision or foliage wind.

This extractor is infrastructure for later bounded cliffs, overhangs, and cave
patches, not an implemented cave system. Future scene authority must send a
compact deterministic field recipe, never a server-generated render mesh.
Authored clips are sampled by the client-owned pose buffer. The semantic router
reads presentation state, resolves weighted clip samples through the animation
pack catalog, and applies fixed-rate FK with per-joint inertialization before
procedural terrain, body-response, and weapon-constraint passes. The validated
server configuration owns each sampling rate and its positive reciprocal.
Buffered sample counts are distinct from elapsed seconds and absolute ticks;
checked interval arithmetic precedes replacement of buffered poses. Inertial
clocks retain checked elapsed time while their polynomial kernels keep the
existing numerical stencil and denominator floors.
Pose buffers distinguish inactive state from retained authored display history.
The first plan snaps to its target; later transitions capture displayed output.
Visibility and physics ownership remain separate: pinning a physics pose does
not establish authored display history. Ordinary locomotion adopts its first
vertical hip correction even at zero elapsed time, then retains that correction
on subsequent zero-elapsed observations.

Shared semantic evaluation and resolved playback carry the same core
`BlendWeight`, `CyclePhase` and `ClipMirror` owners. Weights admit every finite
nonnegative contribution, including values above one; checked accumulation
rejects overflow. Cycles remain finite, signed and unwrapped until a periodic
operation. Mirroring remains binary and serializes as a Boolean. Declared span
endpoints remain in the playback plan even at zero weight; numerical sampling
skips zero contributions. Continuation coordinates and their tangent operations
remain distinct from cyclic phase.

`ClipDuration` admits finite nonnegative seconds, while `ClipTime` admits signed
finite sample positions. Baked clips and both span families retain checked times
and weights until native interpolation or Bevy sampling. Pose interpolation
carries a checked fraction of the fixed sample interval.

The deterministic override stores an `AnimationSampleTick` with the shared
`AnimationElapsed` interval. Repeated observations retain zero elapsed time.
Body response carries finite signed angles, angular velocities and body-local
velocity/acceleration; checked norms and arithmetic remain necessary after
component admission. Failed arithmetic leaves the previous response intact.
Retained run amplitude, authored compensation and landing compression use
nonnegative metre distances; absorption/recovery use nonnegative metre-per-second
rates. Displayed waves and transition offsets use the existing signed metre
owner. Height updates commit only after their checked operations succeed.

Combat YAML owns the observation cap, calibration grid and accepted foot range,
landing tolerances, body-response caps/reference accelerations and safe-settle
interval. Playback drift measurement blending admits only fractions in `[0, 1]`.
Cadence retains checked nonnegative step distances and stance-slip budgets;
selected-axis calibration positions retain signed metres. A fitted phase curve
owns its periodic sample grid and checked seam; an empty or singleton mapping
is explicitly identity, while missing calibration remains absent. Each motion
prepares its fit before replacing its cache entry. Malformed arithmetic is
rejected without marking the clip measured; a valid but unrepresentable fit is
marked observed and uses the simulation profile until its source is invalidated.
Calibration use also checks the relevant runtime tuning and current immutable
rig/retarget offsets before selection. A mismatch excludes that stale entry
until the existing post-sampling calibration pass prepares its replacement;
actor observations, gameplay clocks and unrelated history are retained.
Capture plans and required cadence acceptance propagate distance failures before
publishing their owned plan/report; inspection JSON is prepared separately and
published only after the selected plan succeeds.
The visual root offset uses the existing signed metre owner. Capture frames
retain scenario classification for terrain policy; text is decoded once at
source admission and projected back to labels for authored lookup or reports.

Motion filename stems and asset directories pass checked catalogue admission.
Built-in motions and skeleton families use authored associated constants, while
valid custom identities remain open. A playback plan is admitted after all grip
contributions join; even zero-weight endpoints retain their declared topology.
Clip/source revisions invalidate availability, baked poses, per-character and
shared cadence measurements, phase curves and retained plan keys before new
sampling. Invalid replacement durations remain unavailable until a valid asset
revision arrives. Completed optional requests retain their admitted path even
when no typed handle was returned, so a later managed glTF revision can recover
the same motion by its full asset source, path and label. A failed source or
child clip cannot republish an older asset value as available. This association
does not create a per-frame file retry or a watcher for unrequested assets.
Native asset-store changes invalidate asset-derived pose, stride, phase and
cadence caches before either evaluation or presentation. This conservatively
rebuilds unaffected entries too; native event flushing can cause one additional
rebuild after a real change, while stable frames retain their caches. Actor
observation history and animation clocks are unchanged.

Height amplitudes and speeds share zero-permitting finite measurement leaves.
Body angles retain their signed response-frame role; angular caps use a finite
nonnegative magnitude. Dive, braking and interpolation retain separate roles
over a shared finite unit interval, with each producer keeping its clamp or
rejection policy. Body-response smoothing requires positive seconds; zero now
fails configuration admission before the spring's division. The bake-grid and
phase-fit floors retain their previous values in combat YAML.

Absolute observations use `AnimationSampleTick`; durations use
`AnimationSampleSpan`. Capture increments still wrap, while existing saturated
action/posture deadlines retain their endpoint behavior. Review scenarios carry
admitted execution and acceptance policy through analysis. Captured bones retain
`BoneRole`, and analysis preserves the former lexical report-label order for
floating folds and first-worst ties. Labels and scalar values project at JSON,
HTML, seed and native numerical boundaries. Rejected capture observations write
a failure artifact and terminate instead of retrying the same frame forever.

has its scene attached. The
30fps `AnimationPackCatalog` explicitly owns every semantic pose through a
file/frame anchor and includes unnamed endpoint/closure frames. Source motion
files belong under `assets_src/biped/unarmed/`; `assets_src/base.*` remains the
rig-source special case until `assets_src/biped/unarmed/base.casc` has a

Publish and verify every currently available runtime animation without changing
source exports:

